question: Design a URL shortener like TinyURL or Bit.ly.

collision handling

reference_solution.sample_answer: CAP theorem states a distributed system can only guarantee two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance at once; since network partitions are unavoidable in practice, the real choice is between consistency and availability when a partition occurs. question: Explain consistent hashing and why it's preferred over simple modulo-based hashing for distributed systems.

key_points: hash ring concept mapping nodes and keys to the same space
minimal key remapping when nodes join/leave (only 1/N keys move)
virtual nodes for even load distribution
contrast with modulo hashing (hash % N) which remaps almost all keys on resize

reference_solution.sample_answer: Consistent hashing places both nodes and keys on a conceptual ring using a hash function, and each key is owned by the first node clockwise from its hash position; when a node is added or removed, only the keys between it and its neighbor need to move, unlike modulo hashing (hash(key) % N) where changing N remaps nearly every key. To avoid uneven load from an unlucky node distribution, each physical node is represented by many virtual nodes spread around the ring. This makes it well-suited for distributed caches and sharded storage systems where nodes scale up and down.

question: Explain how database indexing works at scale, including trade-offs of adding indexes.

key_points: B-tree/B+tree indexes for range and point queries

composite/covering indexes for multi-column queries
index selectivity and when an index won't help (low-cardinality columns)
trade-off of storage overhead vs query speed at scale
reference_solution.sample_answer: An index, typically a B+tree, maintains a sorted structure alongside the table so the database can locate rows by a key in O(log n) instead of scanning the full table, which matters enormously at scale. Every index speeds up matching reads but adds write overhead since each insert/update/delete must also update the index structure, and adds storage overhead. Composite indexes covering multiple columns used together in a query can avoid extra lookups, but indexing a low-cardinality column (like a boolean) rarely helps since it doesn't narrow the search much, and over-indexing a write-heavy table can meaningfully degrade write throughput.

question: Explain common rate limiting algorithms (token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window, sliding window) and their trade-offs.

reference_solution.sample_answer: Token bucket allows a burst of requests up to the bucket's capacity while refilling tokens at a steady rate, making it good when occasional bursts are acceptable. question: Explain idempotency in distributed systems and why it matters for reliable APIs.

key_points: idempotent operation: same result no matter how many times it's applied
necessary because networks can cause retries (client timeout, at-least-once delivery)
idempotency keys for non-naturally-idempotent operations like payments

reference_solution.sample_answer: An idempotent operation produces the same end result whether it's executed once or multiple times, which matters because distributed systems retry requests after timeouts even when the original request actually succeeded, risking duplicate side effects. Naturally idempotent operations like a PUT that sets a value are safe to retry, but operations like 'charge $10' aren't idempotent by nature, so clients attach a unique idempotency key and the server stores processed keys with their results, returning the cached result instead of re-executing on a duplicate request. This pattern is essential anywhere at-least-once delivery semantics are used, which is most distributed messaging and retry logic.

question: Explain the difference between eventual consistency and strong consistency, and how to choose between them.

key_points: strong consistency: reads always reflect the latest write
eventual consistency: replicas converge given enough time without new writes
latency/availability benefits of eventual consistency
use cases: strong for financial balances, eventual for like counts/view counts
intermediate models like read-your-own-writes or bounded staleness
reference_solution.sample_answer: Strong consistency guarantees that any read immediately after a write returns that write's value, typically requiring coordination (like quorum reads/writes or a single leader) that adds latency. Eventual consistency only guarantees that replicas will converge to the same value eventually if no new writes occur, trading immediate correctness for lower latency and higher availability, which is fine for data like a social media like count where a few seconds of staleness is invisible to users. The right choice depends on the data: financial balances or inventory counts usually need strong consistency, while activity feeds, view counts, or search index updates can tolerate eventual consistency, and intermediate models like read-your-own-writes offer a middle ground.

question: Compare microservices and monolithic architectures, including when you'd choose each.

key_points: monolith: simpler deployment, easier local development, tighter coupling risk
microservices: independent scaling/deployment, team autonomy, added operational complexity
network calls replace in-process calls, adding latency & failure modes

reference_solution.sample_answer: A monolith bundles all functionality into a single deployable unit, which is simpler to develop, test, and deploy, and avoids network overhead between components, but can become hard to scale or maintain as the codebase and team grow, since everyone shares one deploy cycle and one failure domain. Microservices split functionality into independently deployable services with their own data stores, enabling teams to scale, deploy, and choose tech stacks independently, at the cost of operational complexity: network calls replace function calls (adding latency and new failure modes), and maintaining consistency across service boundaries requires patterns like sagas instead of simple transactions. Microservices tend to pay off at organizational scale with clear domain boundaries and independent teams; a monolith is often the right starting point for small teams or early-stage products.

question: Explain distributed transactions, two-phase commit (2PC), and the saga pattern as alternatives.

key_points: 2PC: coordinator-driven prepare/commit phases across participants
2PC blocks on coordinator failure and doesn't scale well across many services
saga: sequence of local transactions with compensating actions on failure
choreography vs orchestration styles for sagas
sagas trade strict atomicity for availability and scalability
reference_solution.sample_answer: Two-phase commit uses a coordinator that first asks all participants to 'prepare' (lock resources and confirm they can commit), then tells them all to 'commit' or 'abort' based on unanimous agreement, giving atomicity across services but blocking participants (holding locks) if the coordinator crashes mid-protocol, which hurts availability and doesn't scale well across many services or over WAN links. The saga pattern instead breaks a distributed transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with a corresponding compensating action to undo it if a later step fails; sagas can be coordinated by a central orchestrator or via choreography where each service reacts to events from the previous step. Sagas trade strict atomicity (there's a window where partial effects are visible) for much better availability and scalability, which is why most large-scale distributed systems favor sagas over 2PC.

reference_solution.sample_answer: Partitioning is the general concept of splitting a large dataset into smaller pieces, which can happen even within a single database instance (e.g. partitioning a table by date range for query performance). question: Explain how read replicas help scale a database, and what consistency issues they introduce.

reference_solution.sample_answer: Read replicas are copies of the primary database that asynchronously receive updates and serve read traffic, letting you scale reads horizontally by adding more replicas without touching write capacity on the primary. Because replication is typically asynchronous for performance, replicas can lag behind the primary by milliseconds to seconds, meaning a read from a replica might miss a very recent write, which becomes visible as the 'read-your-own-writes' problem when a user updates something and then immediately reads stale data back. Systems often route certain reads (like right after a user's own write) to the primary or a replica known to be caught up, while routing general read traffic to any replica.

question: Explain distributed locking, why it's needed, and the challenges of implementing it correctly (e.g. with Redis or ZooKeeper).

key_points: need: coordinate exclusive access to a shared resource across multiple processes/machines
lock lease/TTL to avoid deadlock if the lock holder crashes

reference_solution.sample_answer: Distributed locking coordinates exclusive access to a shared resource across multiple independent processes or machines, such as ensuring only one instance of a scheduled job runs at a time. Locks are granted with a lease/TTL so a crashed holder doesn't block the resource forever, but this introduces a subtle danger: if the lock holder pauses (e.g. a long GC pause) past the TTL, another process can acquire the lock while the first one is still unaware it lost it, and both may act concurrently. The standard fix is a fencing token, a monotonically increasing number issued with each lock grant, that the protected resource uses to reject writes from a stale, older token, and this is why dedicated coordination services like ZooKeeper or etcd (built on consensus protocols) are often preferred over simpler approaches like Redis's Redlock for correctness-critical locking.

Choosing the timeout is a trade-off: too short and transient network hiccups or GC pauses cause false-positive failure detection, triggering unnecessary failovers, while too long delays real failure detection and recovery. question: Explain quorum-based consistency (the R+W>N rule) and vector clocks for conflict detection in distributed data stores.

key_points: N: total replicas, W: write acknowledgments required, R: read acknowledgments required
R+W>N guarantees read/write quorums overlap, ensuring at least one up-to-date replica is read
tuning R and W trades off latency, consistency, and availability
vector clocks track causal history per replica to detect concurrent (conflicting) writes
vector clocks vs simple timestamps: detect true concurrency, not just chronological order
reference_solution.sample_answer: In a system with N replicas, W is the number of replicas that must acknowledge a write and R the number that must respond to a read; when R+W>N, every read quorum is guaranteed to overlap with every write quorum by at least one replica, so a read will see the latest acknowledged write. Tuning R and W lets you trade latency and availability for consistency: W=N and R=1 gives fast reads but slow, less available writes, while R=1,W=1 is fast both ways but can return stale data. Vector clocks attach a per-replica counter to each version of a value, so when two versions are compared, the system can tell whether one causally preceded the other or whether they were concurrent (a true conflict) — something a plain timestamp can't distinguish due to clock skew across machines.

question: Explain backpressure in distributed systems and strategies for handling it when a consumer can't keep up with a producer.

reference_solution.sample_answer: Backpressure is the mechanism by which an overwhelmed downstream consumer signals upstream producers to slow down, preventing memory exhaustion or cascading failure when production outpaces consumption. question: Explain database normalization vs denormalization and when you'd denormalize for performance at scale.

reference_solution.sample_answer: Normalization organizes data to minimize redundancy by splitting it into related tables (following normal forms), which avoids update anomalies since each fact is stored once, but requires joins to reconstruct a full view, which get expensive at scale, especially across shards. Denormalization intentionally duplicates data (e.g. embedding a user's display name directly in each of their posts) to avoid joins on the read path, trading faster reads for the complexity of keeping duplicated data consistent on writes. question: Explain the circuit breaker pattern and how it prevents cascading failures in distributed systems.

key_points: closed/open/half-open states modeling normal, failing, and probing behavior
trips open after a failure threshold to stop calling a failing dependency
fail-fast behavior protects the caller's own resources (threads/connections) from piling up
half-open state periodically probes if the dependency has recovered
often paired with fallback logic and timeouts/bulkheads for full resilience
reference_solution.sample_answer: A circuit breaker wraps calls to a downstream dependency and tracks failures; in the closed state it allows calls through normally, but once failures exceed a threshold it trips to the open state and fails fast (returning an error or fallback immediately) without even attempting the call, protecting the caller from wasting threads/connections waiting on a struggling dependency and giving the dependency room to recover. After a cooldown period it moves to a half-open state, allowing a limited number of trial requests through to test if the dependency has recovered, closing the circuit again if they succeed or reopening it if they fail. This pattern is central to preventing cascading failures, where one slow/failing service causes callers to pile up resources and become slow/failing themselves.

question: Explain what a Bloom filter is, how it works, and common use cases in large-scale systems.

key_points: probabilistic set-membership structure using a bit array and multiple hash functions
no false negatives, but tunable false positive rate
space-efficient compared to storing the full set
use cases: avoiding unnecessary disk lookups (databases like Cassandra/LevelDB), deduplication in crawlers, cache miss prevention

reference_solution.sample_answer: A Bloom filter is a space-efficient probabilistic data structure for testing set membership: it uses a bit array and several hash functions, setting bits on insertion, and checking membership by verifying all the corresponding bits are set. It never gives false negatives (if it says 'not present,' the element definitely isn't in the set) but can give false positives at a rate tunable by the array size and number of hash functions, and it uses far less memory than storing the actual elements. This makes it useful for avoiding expensive lookups, like checking a Bloom filter before hitting disk in a database (Cassandra/LevelDB use this to skip SSTables that definitely don't contain a key) or checking whether a URL has already been crawled before doing a more expensive lookup.

question: Design a CI/CD deployment pipeline system that builds, tests, and deploys code changes across many services safely.

a rollback mechanism, ideally automatic on failed health checks, is needed so a bad deploy doesn't stay live

reference_solution.sample_answer: A code change triggers a new pipeline run, which executes build and test stages inside isolated, reproducible environments, typically containers, before anything is ever deployed. I'd have a queue of pending pipeline runs backed by a pool of build workers, so many teams' pipelines can run concurrently without blocking each other. The deployment stage should support a gradual rollout strategy like canary or blue-green, with automated health checks gating how much traffic shifts to the new version, rather than cutting over 100% of traffic instantly. If health checks fail during rollout, I'd want an automatic rollback rather than requiring a human to notice and intervene. It's also important to build the deployable artifact, like a container image, exactly once early in the pipeline and reuse that same artifact through every later stage, rather than rebuilding at each stage and risking the tested artifact drifting from what actually gets deployed.

question: Design a time-series metrics monitoring system, similar to Prometheus, that ingests and stores millions of metric data points per second.

key_points: metrics are high-volume, append-only, and time-ordered, which is exploitable for efficient storage (e.g. delta/delta-of-delta encoding for timestamps and values)
data is typically sharded by metric/label combination, letting ingestion scale horizontally across many storage nodes
a write-ahead buffer batches incoming points before flushing them to compressed, immutable time-ordered blocks on disk
older data is often downsampled or aggregated (rolled up) to reduce storage cost, trading precision for retention length
queries need an indexing structure over metric names and labels to quickly find the relevant time series, since scanning everything wouldn't scale
reference_solution.sample_answer: Metrics data is high-volume, append-only, and strictly time-ordered, which lets me use efficient compression like delta-of-delta encoding for timestamps and values, since consecutive points are usually very close to each other. I'd shard data by metric-and-label combination, letting ingestion scale horizontally across many storage nodes without any single node becoming a bottleneck. Incoming points would be batched in a write-ahead buffer and periodically flushed into compressed, immutable time-ordered blocks on disk, which are efficient to write and to later scan sequentially. To control storage growth over time, older data would be downsampled or aggregated into coarser rollups, trading some precision for much longer retention. For queries, I'd maintain an index over metric names and label combinations so a query like 'show me CPU usage for service X' can quickly locate the relevant time series without scanning the entire dataset.

question: Design a distributed tracing system that lets engineers follow a single request's path across dozens of microservices.

key_points: a trace ID is generated at the entry point and propagated through every downstream call (HTTP headers, message metadata) so all services tag their spans with the same trace ID
each service emits spans representing its own unit of work, with a parent-child relationship to the span that called it, forming a tree for the full trace
spans are sent asynchronously to a collector, so tracing instrumentation doesn't add synchronous latency to the actual request path
sampling (recording only a fraction of traces, or biasing toward errors/slow requests) is essential at scale, since storing every span for every request would be prohibitively expensive
a storage and query layer lets engineers look up a trace by ID and visualize the full span tree, along with searching by service, duration, or error status
reference_solution.sample_answer: A trace ID is generated once at the request's entry point and propagated through every downstream call, whether over HTTP headers or message metadata, so every service involved tags its own spans with that same shared trace ID. Each service emits spans representing its own unit of work, each linked to the span that called it, which together form a tree describing the full request's path across every service. Spans are sent asynchronously to a collector rather than synchronously as part of the request, so tracing instrumentation doesn't add latency to the actual user-facing request path. At real scale, I'd apply sampling, recording only a fraction of traces or deliberately biasing toward errors and slow requests, since storing every single span for every request would be prohibitively expensive. Finally, a storage and query layer lets engineers look up a specific trace by ID and visualize its full span tree, or search across traces by service, duration, or error status to find patterns.

question: Design a feature flag service that lets engineers toggle features on and off for specific user segments, instantly, without deploying new code.

evaluating a flag must be extremely fast and reliable, typically done in-process using a local, periodically-refreshed cache of flag configs rather than a network call per evaluation
consistent hashing of a stable user identifier is used for percentage rollouts, so the same user always gets the same variant
an SDK on each application server pulls or is pushed the latest flag configuration and evaluates flags locally against it

reference_solution.sample_answer: Flag configuration, meaning which segments or percentages see which variant, is stored centrally in a config service, and needs to propagate out to every application server quickly. Evaluating a flag has to be extremely fast and can't depend on a network call per evaluation, so each application server would run an SDK holding a local, periodically-refreshed cache of the current flag configuration, evaluating flags entirely in-process against that cache. For percentage-based rollouts, I'd hash a stable user identifier consistently, so the same user always lands in the same bucket and sees the same variant across requests, rather than a random result each time. An SDK on each server either polls the central service periodically or subscribes to push updates for the latest configuration. Since this system can instantly change production behavior for real users, I'd also keep an audit log recording who changed which flag, to what, and when, for accountability and quick rollback investigation.

question: Design the real-time state synchronization system for an online multiplayer game, where many players' actions must be reflected consistently and with low latency for everyone.

key_points: a real-time game typically uses UDP rather than TCP for state updates, tolerating occasional packet loss in exchange for lower latency, since a stale position update is often better than a delayed one
an authoritative game server maintains the true game state and validates client actions, rather than trusting clients directly, to prevent cheating

client-side prediction lets a player's own client immediately show the result of their action locally, before server confirmation, then reconciles/corrects if the server's authoritative result differs
the server periodically broadcasts state snapshots (or deltas) to all connected clients at a fixed tick rate, rather than sending every individual event immediately to everyone
geographically distributing game servers, and matching players to a nearby server, minimizes round-trip latency for real-time responsiveness
reference_solution.sample_answer: I'd use UDP rather than TCP for real-time state updates, tolerating occasional packet loss in exchange for lower latency, since a slightly stale position update generally hurts gameplay less than a delayed one waiting on retransmission. An authoritative game server maintains the true game state and validates every client's submitted actions, rather than trusting clients directly, which is essential for preventing cheating. To keep the game feeling responsive despite network latency, I'd use client-side prediction: a player's own client immediately shows the result of their action locally, before the server has confirmed it, and then reconciles or corrects the display if the server's authoritative outcome ends up differing. The server would broadcast state snapshots or deltas to all connected clients at a fixed tick rate, rather than pushing every individual event to everyone the instant it happens, to bound bandwidth and processing cost. Finally, I'd geographically distribute game servers and match players to a nearby one, since round-trip latency to the server is often the single biggest factor in how responsive the game actually feels.

question: Design the backend for a video conferencing application like Zoom, supporting many participants in a single call with audio and video.

key_points: for small calls, a mesh peer-to-peer topology (everyone connects directly to everyone) works, but doesn't scale past a handful of participants since each client's upload bandwidth grows with participant count

for larger calls, a Selective Forwarding Unit (SFU) server sits in the middle: each participant uploads their stream once to the SFU, which forwards it to every other participant, capping each client's upload cost regardless of call size
media is transmitted over UDP-based protocols (like those underlying WebRTC) for low latency, tolerating some packet loss rather than retransmitting and adding delay
adaptive bitrate lets each participant's stream quality degrade gracefully for viewers on a poor connection, rather than one slow viewer degrading the call for everyone
a separate signaling server handles call setup (who's joining, session negotiation) over a reliable channel, distinct from the actual real-time media path
reference_solution.sample_answer: For small calls, a mesh peer-to-peer topology, where every participant connects directly to every other participant, works fine, but it doesn't scale past a handful of people, since each client's own upload bandwidth has to grow linearly with the number of other participants. For larger calls, I'd use a Selective Forwarding Unit server sitting in the middle: each participant uploads their own stream just once to the SFU, and the SFU forwards it out to every other participant, which caps each client's upload cost at a constant amount regardless of how many people are in the call. Media itself is transmitted over UDP-based protocols, the kind underlying WebRTC, favoring low latency and tolerating some packet loss rather than retransmitting lost packets and adding delay. I'd support adaptive bitrate so each individual participant's stream quality can degrade gracefully specifically for viewers on a poor connection, rather than one slow participant dragging down the call for everyone else. Call setup itself, like negotiating who's joining and exchanging session details, would go through a separate signaling server over a reliable channel, kept distinct from the actual real-time media path.

question: Design a stock exchange's order matching engine, which must match buy and sell orders fairly and with extremely low, predictable latency.

key_points: a single-threaded (or carefully partitioned) matching engine per instrument avoids the coordination overhead and unpredictable latency of locking shared state across multiple threads
the order book is maintained as a price-ordered data structure (e.g. sorted structures per price level) so the best bid/ask can be found and matched extremely quickly
orders are processed strictly in the order they're received (price-time priority) to guarantee fairness: earlier orders at the same price get matched first
every incoming order and every match is written to an append-only log first, for auditability and to allow exact replay/recovery after a crash
matching logic for a single instrument runs in-memory for speed, with the durable log providing crash recovery rather than the hot path depending on synchronous disk writes for every micro-operation
reference_solution.sample_answer: I'd run a single-threaded matching engine per instrument, since introducing locking across multiple threads for shared order book state adds unpredictable latency jitter that's specifically unacceptable for a trading system, where consistent low latency matters as much as raw throughput. The order book for that instrument is maintained as a price-ordered structure, letting the engine find the best bid and best ask and attempt a match extremely quickly. Orders are matched using strict price-time priority: at a given price, whichever order arrived first gets matched first, which is the fairness guarantee traders actually rely on. Every incoming order and every resulting match gets written to an append-only log, both for regulatory auditability and so the exact sequence of events can be replayed to recover state after a crash. The actual matching logic runs entirely in-memory for speed, with that durable log providing crash recovery, rather than the hot matching path itself depending on a synchronous disk write for every single micro-operation.

question: Design a distributed file storage system, similar to HDFS or GFS, that stores huge files reliably across many commodity machines.

key_points: large files are split into fixed-size blocks (e.g. 128MB) distributed across many storage (data) nodes, rather than stored whole on one machine
a metadata/naming service tracks which blocks make up which file and which data nodes currently hold each block, kept separate from the actual bulk data
each block is replicated across multiple data nodes (commonly 3), so losing one machine doesn't lose any data and reads can be served from any healthy replica
the metadata service is a potential single point of failure and bottleneck, so it's typically kept small (metadata only, not data) and made highly available via its own replication

clients talk to the metadata service to find which data nodes hold the blocks they need, then talk directly to those data nodes for the actual bulk data transfer, keeping the metadata service off the data path
reference_solution.sample_answer: Large files are split into fixed-size blocks, commonly around 128MB, and those blocks are distributed across many data nodes rather than any single file living whole on one machine. A separate metadata service tracks which blocks make up which file and which data nodes currently hold each block, keeping that lightweight bookkeeping distinct from the actual bulk data storage. Each block is replicated across multiple data nodes, commonly three, so losing any one machine doesn't lose data, and reads can be served from whichever healthy replica is closest or least loaded. Since the metadata service is a potential single point of failure and bottleneck if every data operation went through it, I'd keep it storing only metadata, never bulk data, and make it highly available through its own replication. Clients talk to the metadata service just to find out which data nodes hold the blocks they need, then talk directly to those data nodes for the actual bulk data transfer, which keeps the metadata service completely off the actual data path and able to handle far more total throughput.

question: Design the backend for a live video streaming platform (like Twitch), where a broadcaster's stream must reach potentially millions of concurrent viewers with low latency.

key_points: the broadcaster's single incoming stream is ingested once, then transcoded into multiple quality/bitrate variants to support viewers on different connection speeds
the transcoded output is split into short segments and distributed through a CDN, so viewers pull segments from a nearby edge server rather than all hitting the origin directly

this segmented, CDN-distributed approach (like HLS/DASH) trades some latency (segment buffering) for massive scalability, since a fan-out to millions of viewers can't realistically be a direct connection per viewer to one origin server
for lower-latency needs, a smaller segment duration reduces the buffering delay, at the cost of more overhead from more frequent segment requests
viewer count and stream metadata need a separate, highly available path so live viewer counts and chat can update quickly, distinct from the actual heavy video data path
reference_solution.sample_answer: The broadcaster's single incoming stream is ingested once at an origin server, then transcoded into multiple quality and bitrate variants, so viewers with different connection speeds can each get an appropriate stream. That transcoded output is split into short segments and distributed out through a CDN, so the vast majority of viewers pull segments from a nearby edge server rather than every single viewer hitting the origin directly, which simply couldn't handle millions of direct connections. This segmented, CDN-distributed approach, similar to HLS or DASH, trades away some latency, since the client buffers a segment or two before playback, in exchange for massive scalability that a direct per-viewer connection to one origin could never achieve. For streams needing lower latency, a smaller segment duration reduces that buffering delay, at the cost of more overhead from viewers requesting segments more frequently. Live viewer count and chat need their own separate, highly available path so they can update quickly and independently, rather than being coupled to the much heavier video segment delivery path.

question: Design the serving layer for a recommendation system that must return personalized recommendations for a user within tens of milliseconds.

key_points: recommendation serving is typically split into a fast candidate generation stage (retrieve a few hundred plausible items cheaply, e.g. via approximate nearest-neighbor search over embeddings) followed by a heavier ranking stage on just those candidates
doing full model inference over the entire item catalog for every request would be far too slow; narrowing to a small candidate set first makes the expensive ranking step tractable
user and item embeddings are precomputed offline in batch jobs and served from a low-latency store at request time, rather than computed fresh per request
a feature store provides consistent, fast-to-fetch features to the ranking model at serving time, avoiding recomputation of expensive features on every request
caching frequently-requested recommendation results (with a reasonably short TTL) reduces load for hot users/contexts while keeping recommendations reasonably fresh
reference_solution.sample_answer: I'd split serving into two stages: a fast candidate generation stage that cheaply retrieves a few hundred plausible items, typically via approximate nearest-neighbor search over precomputed embeddings, followed by a heavier ranking model that only runs on that much smaller candidate set. Running full model inference over an entire catalog of millions of items for every single request would be far too slow, so narrowing down to a small candidate set first is what makes the expensive ranking step actually tractable within the latency budget. Both user and item embeddings are precomputed offline in batch jobs and served from a low-latency store, like a vector database or in-memory cache, at request time, rather than being computed fresh for every single request. A feature store provides the ranking model with consistent, quickly-fetchable features at serving time, avoiding recomputing expensive features on the hot path. I'd also cache the final recommendation results for a reasonably short TTL specifically for hot users or contexts, reducing repeated load while keeping the actual recommendations reasonably fresh.

question: Design a rate-limited proxy service that sits in front of an expensive third-party API, shared across many internal teams, and fairly distributes the third-party's rate limit among them.

key_points: the proxy sits between all internal callers and the third-party API, so it can enforce the third-party's overall rate limit centrally regardless of how many internal teams are calling it
each internal team gets its own sub-quota, tracked centrally, so one team's heavy usage can't starve every other team of the shared external limit
requests exceeding a team's sub-quota (but within the overall limit) are queued or rejected with a clear retry-after signal, rather than being silently dropped
the proxy should cache responses for identical, cacheable requests where appropriate, reducing actual calls to the scarce third-party quota
monitoring per-team usage against their sub-quota and the overall shared limit lets you catch a team about to exhaust the shared resource before it actually happens
reference_solution.sample_answer: I'd route every internal call to the third-party API through this proxy, so it can enforce the third-party's overall rate limit centrally, regardless of how many separate internal teams are actually calling it. Each team would get its own sub-quota, tracked centrally by the proxy, so one team's unexpectedly heavy usage can't starve every other team of their fair share of the shared external limit. Requests exceeding a team's sub-quota, while the overall external limit still has room, would be queued briefly or rejected with a clear retry-after signal, rather than silently dropped with no explanation. Where appropriate, I'd have the proxy cache responses for identical, genuinely cacheable requests, which directly reduces actual calls made against the scarce shared third-party quota. I'd also monitor each team's usage against both their own sub-quota and the overall shared limit, so an on-call engineer can catch a team about to exhaust the shared resource before it actually happens and affects everyone else.

candidates are generated cheaply (e.g. 2-hop graph traversal, capped in size) then ranked by a lighter-weight scoring model considering mutual connections, shared interests, and recency of activity
results should be cached per user with a reasonable refresh interval, since the graph and a user's context don't change meaningfully within short time windows
the suggestion pipeline is largely similar in shape to a general recommendation system: cheap candidate generation followed by ranking, specialized here around graph-structural signals
reference_solution.sample_answer: The follower graph is far too large to traverse live from scratch for every single suggestion request, so I'd rely on precomputed signals for candidate generation, like 'friends of friends' or mutual connection counts, computed in batch jobs ahead of time rather than live. I'd use a graph-aware storage layer, or precomputed and cached adjacency lists for hot, active users, to support fast lookups of who a given user follows without scanning the entire graph structure. Candidates would be generated cheaply, like a capped 2-hop traversal from the user's existing connections, and then ranked by a lighter-weight scoring model considering things like mutual connection count, shared interests, and recency of the candidate's activity. I'd cache the final suggestion results per user with a reasonable refresh interval, since neither the graph structure nor a user's broader context changes meaningfully within short time windows. Overall, this pipeline has a very similar shape to a general recommendation system: cheap candidate generation followed by ranking, just specialized here around graph-structural signals specific to a social network.

question: Design a distributed cron/job scheduler that guarantees each scheduled job runs exactly once at its scheduled time, even as scheduler instances fail and restart.

key_points: running the scheduler on multiple instances for availability risks the exact same job being triggered twice if two instances both believe it's their responsibility to fire it
a distributed lock, or a designated leader elected among the scheduler instances, ensures only one instance is actually responsible for triggering jobs at any given moment

each job execution is tracked with a durable, idempotent 'claim' (e.g. a row with a unique constraint on job-id-plus-scheduled-time) so even a brief overlap during leader failover can't cause a genuine duplicate execution

actual job execution is decoupled from the triggering/scheduling decision: the scheduler enqueues a task, and a separate pool of workers actually executes it, so scheduler failover doesn't affect in-progress job execution

true 'exactly once' is hard to guarantee if the job's own side effect isn't idempotent; the system practically guarantees 'exactly once trigger, with at-least-once delivery to a worker', relying on idempotent job handlers for full correctness
reference_solution.sample_answer: Running the scheduler across multiple instances for availability risks the exact same job firing twice if two instances both believe, even briefly, that it's their job to trigger it. I'd have the scheduler instances elect a single leader, using a distributed lock via something like ZooKeeper or etcd, so only one instance is actually responsible for triggering jobs at any given moment, with a new leader taking over quickly if the current one fails. Each job execution is tracked with a durable, idempotent claim, like a database row with a unique constraint on the combination of job ID and scheduled time, so even a brief overlap during leader failover can't slip through and cause a genuine duplicate trigger. I'd decouple actually executing a job from the scheduling decision itself: the scheduler just enqueues a task when it's due, and a separate pool of workers picks it up and executes it, so scheduler failover doesn't affect a job that's already in progress. It's worth being honest that true exactly-once execution is genuinely hard to guarantee if the job's own side effect isn't idempotent — this design practically guarantees an exactly-once trigger with at-least-once delivery to a worker, which still needs the job handler itself to be idempotent for full end-to-end correctness.

question: Design the indexing pipeline for a web search engine that builds an inverted index over billions of documents.

key_points: documents are processed (tokenized, normalized) and each unique term is mapped to a posting list of documents containing it, forming the core inverted index
building the index at web scale is a massive batch job, typically distributed using a MapReduce-style pipeline: map documents to (term, doc-id) pairs, then reduce/group by term to build posting lists
the index is sharded by term (or by document range) across many machines, so no single machine needs to hold the entire index and query load is distributed
since the web changes constantly, the pipeline needs both a full periodic re-index and an incremental update path for newly crawled or changed documents, rather than only ever rebuilding from scratch
the index also stores auxiliary ranking signals (term frequency, position, document authority) alongside posting lists, since raw presence/absence alone isn't enough for ranking relevant results
reference_solution.sample_answer: Documents get tokenized and normalized, and each unique term is mapped to a posting list of every document containing it, which together forms the core inverted index. Building this at web scale is a massive distributed batch job, structured in a MapReduce-style pipeline: a map phase emits (term, doc-id) pairs for every document, and a reduce phase groups those by term to actually build each term's posting list. The resulting index is sharded, typically by term, across many machines, so no single machine needs to hold the entire index and query load naturally spreads across the shards responsible for whatever terms a given query touches. Since the web is constantly changing, the pipeline needs both a full periodic re-index from scratch and a separate incremental update path for newly crawled or recently changed documents, rather than relying solely on expensive full rebuilds. The index would also store auxiliary ranking signals alongside each posting, like term frequency, term position, and the document's overall authority score, since knowing a term simply appears in a document isn't enough on its own to rank the most genuinely relevant results.

question: Design an uptime/health monitoring service that checks thousands of customer-configured URLs from multiple regions and alerts when one goes down.

key_points: a scheduler triggers checks for each configured URL at its configured interval, distributing the actual checking work across a pool of checker workers, often in multiple geographic regions
checking from multiple regions distinguishes a genuine outage from a localized network problem between one specific checker and the target, avoiding false alarms
a check is only reported as a failure after confirmation from multiple regions (or multiple consecutive failed attempts), reducing false positives from transient blips

results are written to a time-series-like store for historical uptime reporting, and an alerting pipeline evaluates whether a status change (up-to-down) should trigger a notification, respecting configured thresholds and notification channels
the checker fleet itself needs to be horizontally scalable and independently deployable per region, since the number of monitored URLs and check frequency can grow substantially over time
reference_solution.sample_answer: A scheduler triggers a check for each configured URL at its configured interval, distributing the actual check work across a pool of checker workers spread across multiple geographic regions. Checking from multiple regions matters specifically because it lets the system distinguish a genuine outage of the target from a purely localized network problem between just one checker and the target, avoiding false alarms from a regional network blip that isn't the customer's actual problem. I'd only report a real failure after confirmation from multiple regions, or after multiple consecutive failed attempts from the same region, to reduce false positives triggered by a single transient network hiccup. Check results get written to a time-series-oriented store to support historical uptime reporting, and a separate alerting pipeline evaluates whether a status transition, like going from up to down, should actually trigger a notification, respecting each customer's configured thresholds and notification channels. The checker fleet itself needs to scale horizontally and be deployable independently per region, since both the number of monitored URLs and how frequently they're checked can grow substantially as the service gains customers.

question: Design a real-time collaborative code editor that supports syntax highlighting and safe code execution for multiple simultaneous users editing the same file.

key_points: concurrent edits to the same document need a conflict resolution algorithm like Operational Transformation or a CRDT, so simultaneous edits from different users converge to the same consistent final document for everyone
syntax highlighting can run entirely client-side, incrementally re-parsing just the changed region rather than the whole file, keeping it fast enough to run on every keystroke

executing untrusted user code must happen in an isolated sandbox (e.g. a locked-down container or VM) with strict CPU, memory, and time limits, since arbitrary code execution is a serious security risk if not contained

each execution request should be handled by an ephemeral, disposable sandbox instance rather than a long-lived shared one, so one user's misbehaving code can't affect another user's execution or persist unwanted state
the collaborative document state and the code execution path are largely independent subsystems: one handles real-time text synchronization, the other handles isolated, on-demand code running
reference_solution.sample_answer: Concurrent edits from multiple users to the same document need a conflict resolution algorithm, like Operational Transformation or a CRDT, so that simultaneous edits from different users are merged and converge to the exact same consistent final document for everyone, regardless of the order edits actually arrive in. Syntax highlighting can run entirely client-side, incrementally re-parsing just the changed region of the file rather than reparsing the whole thing on every keystroke, which is what keeps it fast enough to actually run continuously as the user types. Executing untrusted user-submitted code has to happen inside an isolated sandbox, like a locked-down container or a lightweight VM, with strict CPU, memory, and wall-clock time limits, since letting arbitrary code run without containment is a serious security risk. I'd give each execution request its own ephemeral, disposable sandbox instance rather than a long-lived shared one, so one user's misbehaving or malicious code can never affect another user's execution or leave unwanted state behind for the next run. The collaborative document state and the code execution path are really two largely independent subsystems here: one handles real-time text synchronization between users, and the other handles isolated, on-demand code running, and they don't need to be tightly coupled together.

question: Design a distributed lock coordination service, similar to ZooKeeper or etcd, that other services rely on for leader election and distributed locking.

key_points: the coordination service itself must be highly available and strongly consistent, so it's typically built on a consensus protocol like Raft or Paxos, replicated across an odd number of nodes to tolerate minority failures

clients acquire a lock by writing a uniquely-named entry (or ephemeral node) that only one client can successfully create at a time, with the consensus layer guaranteeing only one write actually succeeds among concurrent attempts

locks are typically tied to a session with a heartbeat/lease; if the lock holder's session expires (e.g. it crashed and stopped heartbeating), the lock is automatically released so the system doesn't deadlock forever on a dead client

a lock release racing with a lease expiry is a subtle correctness risk: clients should use a fencing token (a monotonically increasing value tied to each lock acquisition) so a downstream resource can detect and reject a stale, delayed operation from a client that has already lost the lock
since correctness matters far more than raw throughput for this service, the write path deliberately favors consistency over availability during a network partition, per the CAP theorem
reference_solution.sample_answer: The coordination service itself has to be highly available and strongly consistent, so I'd build it on a consensus protocol like Raft, replicated across an odd number of nodes so it can tolerate a minority of node failures while still making progress. Clients acquire a lock by attempting to write a uniquely-named entry, and the consensus layer guarantees only one such write actually succeeds among any concurrent attempts, giving exactly one client the lock. Locks would be tied to a session with a heartbeat or lease, so if the lock holder's session expires, for example because it crashed and stopped heartbeating, the lock is automatically released rather than staying held forever and deadlocking every other client waiting on it. A subtle correctness risk is a lock release racing with a lease expiry, so I'd have clients use a fencing token, a monotonically increasing value tied to each lock acquisition, letting a downstream resource detect and reject a stale, delayed operation coming from a client that has actually already lost the lock by the time that operation arrives. Since correctness matters far more than raw throughput for this specific service, the write path deliberately favors consistency over availability during a network partition, consistent with the CAP theorem's trade-off.

question: Design a payment reconciliation system that detects and reports discrepancies between your internal ledger and a payment processor's records.

key_points: both your internal ledger and the payment processor's settlement records need to be treated as append-only, immutable event logs, so reconciliation is comparing two historical records rather than two mutable current states

reconciliation runs as a periodic batch job matching transactions between the two sources by a shared identifier (e.g. a transaction/payment intent ID), flagging anything present in one source but missing or mismatched in the other

matching needs to tolerate expected timing differences (a transaction may settle on the processor's side hours after it was recorded internally), rather than flagging every timing gap as a discrepancy
discrepancies are categorized (missing, amount mismatch, status mismatch, duplicate) and routed to a human review queue or an automated resolution workflow depending on severity and type
the reconciliation system itself must never silently 'fix' financial data automatically without an audit trail, since incorrect automatic correction of money-related records is a serious risk
reference_solution.sample_answer: Both the internal ledger and the payment processor's own settlement records should be treated as append-only, immutable event logs, so reconciliation becomes a matter of comparing two historical records rather than trying to compare two mutable, currently-changing states. I'd run reconciliation as a periodic batch job that matches transactions between the two sources by a shared identifier, like a transaction or payment intent ID, flagging anything present in one source but missing or mismatched in the other. The matching logic needs to tolerate expected timing differences, since a transaction might genuinely settle on the processor's side hours after it was first recorded internally, so I wouldn't flag every timing gap as a real discrepancy, only ones that persist past a reasonable settlement window. Discrepancies would be categorized, like missing, amount mismatch, status mismatch, or duplicate, and routed either to a human review queue or an automated resolution workflow depending on the severity and type of the specific discrepancy. Critically, the system should never silently 'auto-fix' financial records without a clear audit trail, since an incorrect automatic correction to money-related data is a genuinely serious risk that needs human oversight.

question: Design a real-time fraud detection pipeline for an e-commerce checkout flow that must approve or flag transactions within a few hundred milliseconds.

key_points: a tight latency budget rules out anything requiring a slow batch computation at request time; features and model inference both need to be fast, low-single-digit-millisecond operations

real-time features (e.g. transaction velocity for this card/user in the last few minutes) are maintained incrementally in a fast in-memory store, updated as events stream in, rather than recomputed from scratch per request

a fast, cheap rules-based or lightweight model layer handles the bulk of clearly-legitimate or clearly-fraudulent transactions instantly, escalating only genuinely ambiguous cases to a heavier model or human review, to keep the common-case latency low

the system must fail safe: if the fraud-check service itself is slow or unavailable, there needs to be a defined fallback policy (e.g. default-allow with heavier post-hoc review, or default-deny) rather than the checkout flow hanging indefinitely

labels for whether a flagged transaction was truly fraudulent often arrive much later (chargebacks take weeks), so the pipeline needs a separate feedback loop to retrain models on delayed ground truth
reference_solution.sample_answer: Given the tight latency budget, I'd rule out anything requiring slow computation at request time — both feature lookups and model inference need to be fast, low-single-digit-millisecond operations. Real-time features, like this card or user's transaction velocity over the last few minutes, are maintained incrementally in a fast in-memory store, updated continuously as events stream in, rather than recomputed from scratch for every single incoming request. I'd put a fast, cheap rules-based or lightweight model layer in front to handle the bulk of clearly-legitimate or clearly-fraudulent transactions instantly, only escalating genuinely ambiguous cases to a heavier model or a human review queue, which keeps the common-case latency low while still catching harder cases with more scrutiny. The system needs to fail safe: if the fraud-check service itself becomes slow or unavailable, there has to be a defined fallback policy, like defaulting to allow with heavier post-hoc review, rather than letting the checkout flow hang indefinitely waiting on a check that might never come back. Since ground-truth labels for whether a flagged transaction was truly fraudulent often only arrive weeks later through chargebacks, I'd also build a separate feedback loop feeding that delayed ground truth back into model retraining.

question: Design a real-time ad bidding system that must select and price an ad to display within roughly 100 milliseconds of a page load, with many advertisers bidding simultaneously.

key_points: the 100ms budget is a hard constraint that shapes the whole design: the request fans out to many bidders in parallel, and a strict timeout collects whichever bids arrived in time rather than waiting for stragglers
bidder eligibility (targeting rules, budget remaining) is pre-filtered as cheaply as possible before the actual bid computation, so expensive bid logic only runs for genuinely eligible advertisers

an auction mechanism (commonly a second-price auction) determines the winning bid and the actual price charged, which is designed to incentivize bidders to bid their true value rather than gaming the price

advertiser budgets need to be tracked and decremented in near-real-time across many concurrent auctions, since overspending a budget due to lag in budget tracking is a direct financial correctness problem
any bidder that times out or fails is simply excluded from that specific auction rather than blocking or slowing down the overall auction for everyone else
reference_solution.sample_answer: The roughly 100 millisecond budget is a hard constraint shaping this whole design: an incoming ad request fans out to many potential bidders in parallel, and after a strict timeout, whichever bids actually arrived in time are collected for the auction, with any straggler bidder simply excluded from that specific auction rather than the whole process waiting on it. Before even reaching the actual bid computation, I'd cheaply pre-filter bidder eligibility based on targeting rules and remaining budget, so the more expensive per-bidder bid logic only ever runs for advertisers who are genuinely eligible to participate at all. An auction mechanism, commonly a second-price auction, determines both the winning bid and the actual price charged, which is specifically designed to incentivize bidders to bid their true value rather than trying to game the final price they'll actually pay. Advertiser budgets need to be tracked and decremented in near-real-time across potentially thousands of concurrent auctions happening simultaneously, since any meaningful lag in budget tracking directly risks overspending a budget, which is a real financial correctness problem, not just a performance nuisance.

follow_up_hint: Ask why a second-price auction is commonly used here instead of simply charging the winning bidder their own full bid amount.

question: Design a global username/handle reservation system that guarantees no two users can ever claim the exact same username, even under highly concurrent signups.

sharding this table by a hash of the username (rather than by user ID) keeps the uniqueness check local to a single shard, avoiding a cross-shard coordination protocol for every signup
a 'reserve, then confirm' two-step flow (briefly hold a username during signup, release it if the rest of signup fails) avoids permanently losing a username to an abandoned, incomplete signup

case-insensitivity and lookalike-character normalization (e.g. treating visually similar Unicode characters as equivalent) need to be applied consistently before the uniqueness check, or two visually-identical usernames could otherwise both be accepted as 'unique'
this is fundamentally a strong-consistency problem, not an eventual-consistency one, since even a brief window allowing two users to believe they both got the same name is unacceptable

I'd shard this specific table by a hash of the username itself, rather than by user ID, so the uniqueness check for any given username stays entirely local to one shard, avoiding needing a cross-shard coordination protocol on every single signup. I'd use a 'reserve, then confirm' two-step flow, briefly holding a username during the rest of the signup process and releasing it automatically if signup fails or times out, so a username doesn't get permanently locked away by an abandoned, incomplete signup attempt. Fundamentally, this is a strong-consistency problem, not something you'd want to solve with eventual consistency, since even a brief window where two users could both believe they'd claimed the exact same name is genuinely unacceptable here.

question: Design a distributed counter service that can increment a 'likes' count on a popular post millions of times per second without the counter itself becoming a bottleneck.

key_points: a single row/counter being incremented by millions of concurrent writers becomes a serious write-contention bottleneck, since every increment has to serialize against every other increment to that same row

a sharded counter splits one logical counter into many physical sub-counters (e.g. across N shards), with each increment going to a randomly or consistently chosen shard, spreading write contention across all of them

reading the current total requires summing all shards, which is more expensive than reading a single value, so the total is often cached and refreshed periodically rather than recomputed from all shards on every single read

for extremely high write rates, increments can be batched in memory for a short window (e.g. in a local buffer or a fast in-memory store) and periodically flushed as a single aggregated increment to durable storage, rather than persisting every single increment individually

exact real-time precision is often relaxed intentionally (showing an approximate, slightly-delayed count) in exchange for much higher write throughput, since a 'likes' count doesn't usually need to be perfectly exact to the second
reference_solution.sample_answer: A single row or counter being incremented by millions of concurrent writers becomes a serious write-contention bottleneck, since every single increment effectively has to serialize against every other increment hitting that exact same row. I'd use a sharded counter instead, splitting one logical counter into many physical sub-counters, with each individual increment routed to a randomly or consistently chosen shard, spreading the write contention across all of them rather than concentrating it on one row. Reading the current total then requires summing across all the shards, which is meaningfully more expensive than reading one single value, so I'd cache that total and refresh it periodically rather than recomputing the full sum from every shard on every single read request. For extremely high write rates, I'd also batch increments in memory for a short window, in a local buffer or a fast in-memory store, and periodically flush a single aggregated increment to durable storage, rather than persisting every individual increment one at a time. In exchange for much higher write throughput, I'd intentionally relax exact real-time precision, showing an approximate, slightly-delayed count, since a likes count generally doesn't need to be perfectly exact to the second for users to trust it.

question: Design an image and video processing pipeline that generates multiple thumbnail sizes and formats for every piece of media uploaded to a photo-sharing app.

Processing for the same upload can be parallelized across different output sizes and formats, since generating a small thumbnail doesn't depend at all on a large one being generated first, letting multiple workers process the same upload's different outputs concurrently. The pipeline needs a retry-with-backoff strategy for transient failures, like a worker crashing partway through a job, and a dead-letter path specifically for uploads that consistently fail processing, like a genuinely corrupted file, so those don't just retry forever. Clients should see the original media available quickly, with derived thumbnails progressively becoming available as they finish, rather than the whole upload flow blocking on every single derived asset completing before showing anything at all.

question: Design a multi-region active-active database replication setup for a global application, and explain how you'd handle a write conflict when the same record is updated in two regions nearly simultaneously.

key_points: in active-active, every region accepts writes locally for low regional latency, then asynchronously replicates those writes to every other region, rather than routing all writes through one designated primary region
since writes happen locally and replicate asynchronously, two regions can genuinely accept conflicting concurrent writes to the same record before either has seen the other's update

conflict resolution needs an explicit strategy: last-write-wins by timestamp is simple but can silently lose a legitimate update; a vector clock or version-based approach can at least detect that a conflict happened, even if resolving it still needs care
for some data (e.g. a shopping cart, or an additive counter), a merge function that combines both concurrent updates meaningfully is preferable to picking just one and discarding the other entirely

partitioning writes by data ownership (e.g. a given user's data is always written in their home region) avoids most conflicts entirely for data that doesn't genuinely need cross-region concurrent writes, reserving full conflict resolution for the smaller subset of data that does
reference_solution.sample_answer: In an active-active setup, every region accepts writes locally, which keeps write latency low for users in that region, and those writes then replicate asynchronously out to every other region, rather than every write having to route through one single designated primary region first. question: Design a search-as-you-type autocomplete system that must tolerate typos and return relevant suggestions within tens of milliseconds.

key_points: a trie (prefix tree) over popular queries or terms supports fast exact-prefix lookups, returning top-ranked completions for a given prefix quickly

typo tolerance requires more than exact prefix matching; common approaches include indexing n-grams of each term, or precomputing a bounded edit-distance neighborhood, so a misspelled prefix can still match nearby correct terms
candidate results are ranked by a combination of popularity/frequency and, if available, personalization signals, rather than a single global ranking for everyone

the entire suggestion index (or its hot, frequently-queried portion) is typically kept in memory across replicated servers, since disk-based lookups would be too slow for a per-keystroke latency budget
the index needs periodic refreshing to incorporate newly trending queries, trading index freshness against the cost of frequent rebuilds
reference_solution.sample_answer: I'd build a trie, a prefix tree, over popular queries or terms, which supports fast exact-prefix lookups, quickly returning top-ranked completions for whatever prefix the user has typed so far. Since a trie alone only handles exact prefix matches, typo tolerance needs something more, like indexing n-grams of each term or precomputing a bounded edit-distance neighborhood around common terms, so a slightly misspelled prefix can still successfully match nearby, correctly-spelled terms. Candidate results would be ranked by a combination of overall popularity or query frequency, and personalization signals where available, rather than showing the exact same global ranking to every single user regardless of their own history. The entire suggestion index, or at least its hot, frequently-queried portion, would be kept in memory across replicated servers, since disk-based lookups would simply be too slow to fit within a per-keystroke latency budget of tens of milliseconds. question: Design the backend for an online auction system (like eBay) that handles competitive bidding on items ending at a specific time, including last-second 'sniping' bids.

key_points: concurrent bids on the same item at the same moment need atomic, serialized processing (e.g. optimistic locking with a version check, or routing all bids for one item through a single ordering point) so two simultaneous bids can't both be accepted as the new current-highest

a bid is only accepted if it exceeds the current highest bid at the moment it's actually processed, so the system needs to re-check that condition atomically rather than trusting a stale 'current highest' the client saw earlier

auction end time needs careful handling for last-second bids ('sniping'): a bid received a moment before the deadline must still be validly processed and reflected before the auction is finalized, requiring the closing logic to wait for genuinely in-flight bids rather than cutting off abruptly at a wall-clock instant

auto-bidding (a user sets a max bid and the system bids incrementally on their behalf up to that max) adds logic that must also respect the same atomic highest-bid-check to avoid inconsistent outcomes
notifying outbid users in near-real-time (so they can respond before the auction closes) requires a fast fan-out from the bid-processing path, distinct from the durable bid-recording path
reference_solution.sample_answer: Concurrent bids arriving for the same item at nearly the same moment need atomic, serialized processing, either via optimistic locking with a version check on the item's current highest bid, or by routing all bids for a given item through a single ordering point, so two simultaneous bids can never both be accepted as the new current-highest bid. A bid should only be accepted if it actually exceeds the current highest bid at the exact moment it's processed, so the check-and-accept has to happen atomically rather than trusting a 'current highest' value the bidder's client saw slightly earlier, which could already be stale. Auction end time needs particularly careful handling for last-second sniping bids: a bid received just before the deadline must still be validly processed and reflected in the final result, which means the closing logic needs to wait for genuinely in-flight bids to finish processing rather than cutting off abruptly the instant the wall clock hits the deadline. Auto-bidding, where a user sets a maximum and the system bids incrementally on their behalf up to that ceiling, needs to go through that exact same atomic highest-bid-check logic to avoid inconsistent outcomes between auto-bids and manual bids. I'd also fan out near-real-time notifications to outbid users through a fast, separate path from the durable bid-recording path, so they have a real chance to respond before the auction actually closes.

question: Design a dynamic surge pricing system for a ride-sharing app that adjusts prices in real time based on current supply and demand in a given area.

a streaming aggregation pipeline continuously updates a supply-demand ratio per cell as driver locations and ride requests stream in, rather than recomputing pricing from scratch on a slow batch schedule
a pricing multiplier is computed per cell from that ratio, with smoothing (e.g. capping how fast the multiplier can change) to avoid jarring, whiplash price swings for users within a short window

the multiplier for a specific ride must be locked in and honored at the moment a rider requests a quote, even if the underlying supply-demand ratio changes moments later, to avoid a rider being charged a different price than they were shown

boundary effects between adjacent cells (a big price jump crossing an arbitrary cell boundary) need smoothing, e.g. by blending neighboring cells' ratios, rather than treating each cell in complete isolation
reference_solution.sample_answer: I'd divide the service area into small geographic cells, using something like a geospatial grid or hexagonal tiling, and track supply, meaning available nearby drivers, and demand, meaning current ride requests, per cell in near-real-time. A streaming aggregation pipeline continuously updates each cell's supply-demand ratio as driver location updates and ride requests stream in, rather than recomputing pricing on some slow batch schedule that would make prices feel stale relative to actual conditions. From that ratio, I'd compute a pricing multiplier per cell, with smoothing that caps how fast the multiplier is allowed to change, to avoid jarring, whiplash price swings for riders within a short time window. Critically, the multiplier shown to a specific rider for their specific quote has to be locked in and honored at that exact moment, even if the underlying supply-demand ratio shifts moments later, so a rider is never actually charged a different price than what they were shown when they requested the ride. I'd also smooth out boundary effects between adjacent cells, for instance by blending in neighboring cells' ratios somewhat, rather than treating each cell as a completely isolated, independent price zone that could jump sharply right at an arbitrary cell boundary.

question: Design a distributed configuration management service that lets application servers fetch and be notified of configuration changes without restarting.

key_points: configuration is stored centrally with versioning, so any change creates a new version rather than overwriting history, supporting audit and rollback to a known-good previous version

application servers hold a local, in-memory cache of the current configuration, refreshed via either periodic polling or a push notification (e.g. long-polling or a pub/sub subscription) when a change occurs, so config reads never block on a network call
changes should roll out gradually (e.g. to a small percentage of servers first) rather than instantly to every server at once, limiting the blast radius of a bad configuration change

the config service itself needs to be highly available, since if it becomes unreachable, application servers should keep serving with their last-known-good cached configuration rather than failing outright
validating a new configuration's schema/values before it's actually published prevents an obviously broken config from ever propagating to production servers in the first place
reference_solution.sample_answer: Configuration is stored centrally with versioning, so every change creates a new version rather than silently overwriting history, which supports both auditing who changed what and rolling back to a known-good previous version if a change turns out to be bad. Application servers hold a local, in-memory cache of the current configuration, refreshed either through periodic polling or a push notification, like long-polling or a pub/sub subscription, when a change actually occurs, so ordinary config reads never have to block on a network call to the central service. I'd roll out configuration changes gradually, to a small percentage of servers first before the rest, rather than pushing a change instantly to every single server at once, which limits the blast radius if a change turns out to have unexpected problems. The config service itself needs to be highly available, and if it does become unreachable for some reason, application servers should just keep serving using their last-known-good cached configuration rather than failing outright. I'd also validate a new configuration's schema and values before it's ever actually published, which prevents an obviously broken configuration from propagating out to production servers in the first place.

question: Design a service discovery system that lets microservices dynamically find healthy instances of the services they depend on, as instances are added, removed, or fail.

instances send periodic heartbeats to the registry; missing several consecutive heartbeats causes the registry to mark that instance as unhealthy and stop returning it to callers, without waiting for a slow, explicit deregistration

callers either query the registry directly (client-side discovery) or go through a load balancer/proxy that itself queries the registry (server-side discovery), each with different coupling trade-offs for the calling service
the registry itself needs to be highly available and reasonably fast to query, since a registry outage could otherwise prevent every service from finding its dependencies at once
clients typically cache the last known set of healthy instances locally for a short period, so a brief registry hiccup doesn't immediately break every dependent service's ability to make calls
reference_solution.sample_answer: A central service registry tracks which instances currently exist for each service, with every instance registering itself on startup and being removed from the registry on a clean shutdown. Instances also send periodic heartbeats to the registry, and missing several consecutive heartbeats causes the registry to mark that specific instance as unhealthy and stop returning it to callers, without needing to wait on a slow or potentially-never-arriving explicit deregistration from a crashed instance. Callers can either query the registry directly themselves, which is client-side discovery, or go through a load balancer or proxy that itself queries the registry on their behalf, which is server-side discovery, and each approach has different coupling trade-offs for the calling service's own code. The registry itself needs to be highly available and fast to query, since an outage there could otherwise prevent every single service from finding its dependencies all at once. I'd also have clients cache the last known set of healthy instances locally for a short period, so a brief registry hiccup doesn't immediately break every dependent service's ability to make calls at all.
